agree.reason: The lost hospital bids and the partners committing to all three days give most staff a reason to go along, but the eleven remote hires who live within two hours get nothing beyond the commuting subsidy, so the ones who stay mainly for remote work may still push back or leave.

honest.reason: Every figure matches what the writer was given, and the claim that working apart causes the slower progression is correctly hedged as 'we think'; the only additions are the inferred 2027/2028 dates and a general statement about how people learn to lead.

works_the_facts.reason: The numbers are repeated as given, not worked out: the memo never says that 15 of 46 is about a third of the firm, never puts the 30% into months or years of delay, and never says what continuing to lose bids would cost.

right_comparison.reason: It implies that staying remote means more lost interviews and slower development, and the five of six leads already in three days helps, but it never sets out the status quo or its trend as a real alternative.

qualification.reason: The six-month review has no date (around March 2028), no measure of success such as bid results or time to lead, and no stated consequence, so readers cannot check it.

objections.reason: It says plainly that the remote hires' terms are changing and deals with the desk and commuting concerns ahead of time, but it doesn't answer 'why three days and not fewer' or say anything to remote hires who live close but still face a real change to their lives.

fit.reason: It's a short, clear email of about one page that points to Friday's meeting and to who can take questions before it, as asked.
